title: NAM Launches 'Industry on Parade': Corporate Television Propaganda Campaign
description: The National Association of Manufacturers launches 'Industry on Parade,' a 13.5-minute weekly television series that runs from 1950-1960, producing over 500 episodes. NAM collaborates with NBC (1950-1953) and later with Arthur Lodge Productions (1953-1960), distributing episodes at no charge to one television station in each market throughout the country, typically in non-prime time slots. By 1957, the show broadcasts on 270 stations nationally and in 33 countries. Each episode features 3-4 stories on American manufacturing, prominently including anti-communist messages and 'public service announcements' promoting capitalism, 'the American way,' and the rewards of a free economy. The series receives a Peabody Award for National Public Service in 1954, providing legitimacy to corporate propaganda. The show promotes capitalist industrial production with such effectiveness that the AFL-CIO demands its own television time, obtaining 'Americans at Work' as a counter-program. This represents sophisticated corporate use of mass media for ideological influence, demonstrating NAM's propaganda infrastructure 21 years before the Powell Memo. The 428-reel collection is now held at the Smithsonian.

significance: Demonstrates NAM's early mastery of television as propaganda tool, reaching millions of viewers across 270 U.S. stations and 33 countries. The program's Peabody Award shows how corporate messaging achieved mainstream legitimacy. AFL-CIO's defensive response ('Americans at Work') shows labor forced to react to corporate media dominance. This 10-year, 500-episode campaign represents unprecedented investment in shaping public opinion about capitalism and free enterprise, establishing template for corporate ideological messaging that continues today.
